capabilities.target: Postgres database via service role (bypasses row level security), including the integration_tokens table and ticket tables
support_messages table (insert), visible to the customer in the ticket thread

inputs.source: Developer's natural-language request in the IDE chat (e.g. 'Show me the latest open support tickets')
Customer-authored ticket message submitted through the public support widget, stored as row content the agent reads
Tool name, description, and schema served by the Supabase MCP server package, fetched fresh via `npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest` on each invocation

controls.name: IDE per-call tool approval prompt (shows raw SQL)
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model; the SQL text shown does not itself depend on model cooperation. However, its real-world effectiveness depends on reviewer attention, which degrades with approval volume (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403) -- an effect the dependence classification alone does not capture.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting credential excluding sensitive tables
controls.decay_rationale: A credential that structurally cannot read integration_tokens makes that data unreachable from this path regardless of model behavior or injected instructions.

controls.name: Content/destination check before inserting into customer-visible support_messages
controls.decay_rationale: Pattern or DLP-style checks on outgoing content can be evaded by a capable model instructed to encode or reformat exfiltrated data before insertion.

controls.name: Prompt-injection classifier/sanitizer on ticket content
controls.decay_rationale: The classifier sees content, not intent; multi-step, encoded, or novel injection phrasing can pass it, and it does not scale with a stronger attacker-crafted injection.

controls.name: Pin and hash the MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: A version/hash check is enforced at deploy time, independent of model behavior, and directly counters rug-pull style definition changes (SAFE-T1201).

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): ticket-injected instructions use the service-role connection to copy integration tokens into a customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Customer submits a ticket message via the public support widget containing hidden instructions directing the agent to also query integration_tokens and include results in its reply.
Agent executes SQL as the service role (bypasses row level security) to read open tickets, ingests the injected instruction, and issues a further query against integration_tokens.
Developer is shown the raw SQL for each call and approves it; with many approvals per session, an additional or disguised query blends into routine approvals (approval fatigue).
Agent inserts the queried integration token values into support_messages as part of the ticket reply.
The customer who authored the original ticket reads the reply and receives the exfiltrated integration tokens.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

findings.residual_rationale: Crediting ctl.tool_call_prompt as a raw_action human approval gate (-2 tiers from critical) would give a naive floor of moderate. The runtime notes state developers approve many calls in a session; that is the approval-fatigue pattern in control_decay.md and SAFE-T1403, under which a routine-looking SQL call is approved without the payload's semantics being scrutinized even though it is shown raw. This volume effect is not expressible in the approval_review_mode field, so residual is rated high rather than moderate.

forecast.watch_signal: IDE or developer settings change to auto-approve tool calls (e.g. 'always allow execute_sql'), or the per-call approval step is disabled or batch-approved, removing per-call raw SQL review.

evidence.observation: Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget, and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, creating an untrusted-input-to-customer-visible-egress path.
The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database as the ticket data the agent is asked to read.
Developers approve many calls in a session, which is the approval-fatigue condition that weakens even a raw-SQL-shown approval gate.

recommendations.action: Scope the Supabase MCP connection to a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role that excludes integration_tokens (and any other credential-bearing table) so ticket-handling queries cannot reach token data regardless of agent or developer behavior.
Add a check before any insert into support_messages that blocks or requires secondary review when the value being written matches patterns from sensitive tables (tokens, secrets, credentials).
Sanitize or spotlight ticket content before it enters agent context (quote/delimit it, strip instruction-like phrasing) and run an injection classifier on it.
Cap approvals per session/time window and require brief justification for any execute_sql call touching sensitive tables, to counter approval fatigue.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server (ASI04): @latest fetch of the Supabase MCP package undermines the integrity of the raw-SQL approval shown to the developer

attack_path.note: The Supabase MCP server package is fetched via `npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest` on each invocation, with no version pin or hash.
Tool names, descriptions, and schemas served by the package can change between sessions without any config change or review on the agent side.
A poisoned or rug-pulled release could alter how execute_sql reads are constructed or labeled, including reads against integration_tokens.

Approval relies on the SQL text and description rendered by the client; an unverified, unpinned server undermines the assumption that what is displayed accurately and consistently reflects what will execute.
A compromised tool definition could reproduce or extend the same exfiltration-to-customer-reply pattern as finding f1, or add an entirely different channel.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

findings.residual_rationale: Crediting ctl.tool_call_prompt alone would give a naive floor of moderate (critical -2 tiers for a raw_action gate). But the same approval-fatigue dynamic noted in f1 applies here, compounded by definitions_pinned: false meaning the integrity of what is displayed cannot be verified session to session (SAFE-T1201). These two facts together are not expressible in the control's dependence field alone, so residual is rated high.

forecast.watch_signal: MCP server package version or hash changes between sessions without an explicit review step, or the per-call approval prompt is disabled.

evidence.observation: mcpServers.supabase runs via `npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest`, with no version pin or hash, so served tool definitions can change between invocations without review.
The developer-facing approval step depends on the SQL shown being an accurate and stable representation of what runs; nothing in the design verifies the server's identity or definitions.

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific version and verify it by checksum/hash before each deployment; fail closed on mismatch.
Diff and log tool definitions/descriptions on each MCP client connection; alert on any change.
Mirror the MCP server package internally rather than fetching @latest from the public registry at runtime.

rating.rationale: Both findings start at critical inherent risk: an untrusted source (customer ticket content in f1, unpinned server-delivered tool definitions in f2) reaches a severe sink (service-role read of restricted integration tokens, chained into an irreversible, customer-visible egress write). The only present control, a per-call raw-SQL approval prompt, earns a two-tier credit by rubric, but the design's own stated approval volume ('developers approve many calls in a session') is the approval-fatigue condition that undermines a raw_action gate in practice, so residual is held at high rather than the naive moderate floor for both findings. Under autonomy_increase, control_removal, or model_upgrade, that same gate is expected to fail outright, returning both findings to critical -- which is why rating.forecast is critical. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctl.tool_call_prompt.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt or agent instructions were provided for ide-db-agent; the declared autonomy level (A1, approval each step) is taken as stated in the runtime notes and was not independently verified.
No logging, audit trail, or anomaly-detection configuration was described, so detective controls could not be evaluated beyond noting their absence.
Confidence on finding f2 is low because no evidence of an actual compromised or rug-pulled package was provided; the finding rests on the absence of version pinning in the configuration artifact.
